The prince’s face suddenly brightened as he responded:

“Do you know, Anna Pávlovna, that I have always looked on my
children as a great misfortune and so I have always felt compassion
for them? I think it is a great misfortune for a man to have children.”

However, the prince’s face still brightened so that it was hard to
believe that he could ever have felt anything but joy and happiness
when he had such children.

“You have a daughter,” said Anna Pávlovna, “who is loved by everyone,
and who will soon be the wife of the Dukes of Kázań. The young
prince is a charming young man. He is going to be a great Duke.”

“He has a good heart and a good head,” said the prince. “But he is
not a good son-in-law. I have told him so.”

“Who, you? Don’t you know that he is a prince of the royal family?
Well, I don’t blame you. I am not a Russian. I have always said that
you are a very good father. I’m not sure that your son-in-law is the
least bit good, but I don’t often find men who are good. My daughter
is charming, and so I think she will be happy.”

The prince began to laugh and said:

“Very well, very well, I don’t dispute your judgment on my son-in-law.
You are right, he is not a good son-in-law—but I have a son whom I
love dearly, and whom I want to protect. I have a son whom I love
dearly, and whom I want to protect. His name is Count Boris Andreyevich
Kurágin.”

And the prince began to tell a story in that slow, impassioned,
languid, and plaintive way of his which was so characteristic of him.
Boris Andreyevich Kurágin, the subject of his story, was a man of
great talent, and had been to Paris. He had been an admirer of Mme
Hélène, the wife of the Prince de Mortemart, whom Anna Pávlovna had
just mentioned, and who was the mistress of the British ambassador,
John Hope. She was passionately adored by a virtuoso in the court
orchestra, Countess Vasiliev, who had just returned from Paris. She
would take him into her carriage, and when she would refuse, she would
insist that he pay for her carriage and horses, and he would give it
her. He often wrote his letters in French, and his letters, which were
short, were full of delicate, pathos-laden, and passionate descriptions
of the joys he was experiencing.

Boris Andreyevich’s letters were so touching that Anna Pávlovna
Schérer, in the midst of the political conversation, seized the
opportunity to give her opinion of him, which was the only one she
had ever heard.

“Such a man,” she said, “has no right to be a member of the
court, no right to be known to the court, no right to be known to
the people, no right to speak of love in letters. There must be a
discipline in Russia.”

Anna Pávlovna’s tone was so severe that the prince had to laugh.

“Anna Pávlovna, don’t come to me with your rules. She is only a
young lady. She is not yet a member of the court. She is still a girl,
and a girl has every right to enjoy her pleasures. I told her so,
though she had a good head, and she made me angry. She is a charming
little creature, but she will never get on with me.”

“I don’t believe she will.”

“I don’t blame her,” said the prince, “I don’t blame her. She is
young.”

“Anna Pávlovna,” said the prince, “if you don’t wish me to
discuss a subject of such importance with you, I’ll take my leave. I
don’t want to leave on bad terms. I’ll give you my word of honor.”

“I don’t know what I was saying. I’m a great enthusiast,” said Anna
Pávlovna, who had been absorbed in recalling her own youthful
passion.

She looked at him in an angry and reproachful manner, and he, smiling,
obviously ready to think of some reply, did not speak.

“I don’t like him,” she added, smiling with a gracious show of
indifference.

“Dear prince, you are ridiculous. If there is anything in the world
I don’t like, and I have a right to speak of it, it is your father.
You are his only son, and so it is a great comfort to me that he
is not alive.”

She suddenly ceased speaking and looked at him with a reproachful
expression. She was right, and the prince, who had no more children,
came to the rescue of his father.

“You will not say that,” he said with a smile. “All my life I
have loved my father. And if there is a living being in the world who
deserves and may be loved by his son, it is he.”

“Do you think so?” said Anna Pávlovna in a reproachful manner.
“Perhaps you are mistaken. I am sure you are mistaken. Vladimir
Mikhailovich always loved his father. I saw him, and I saw his
goodness. You are a good son, Vasíli, but your father is not a
good father.”

“Your father is not a good father?” said the prince. “You
are a fool, Anna Pávlovna.”

“You are a fool. I have told you that Vladimir Mikhailovich loved
his father. You cannot love him. You are not a good son.”

The prince did not reply, but the sensation of his discomfiture
manifested itself in his face. He had been accustomed to always
converse with this woman, and to speak to her as if she were a child,
as if she could not understand what he said. But the Atticus-like
Prince Vasíli was not a fool, and he knew by experience that the
invariable womanly method of rebuking him was to bring him to tears by
a reproach or a pun.

“I am not a good son?” he said in a stentorian tone, with a
performance resembling a cough. “I am not a son of the Emperor
Alexandre? I am a son of the Emperor Alexander? I am a son of the
Emperor Alexander, who, as all know, is the greatest of sovereigns
on earth, who has annihilated the monster of the Revolution and,
perhaps, will be the scourge of the Revolution. And Vladimir
Mikhailovich is my brother, and I am not a good son of the Emperor
Alexander? I am a son of the Emperor Alexander who, perhaps, is
to rule the world? And Vladimir Mikhailovich is my brother? And I
am not a good son of the Emperor Alexander? And Vladimir
Mikhailovich is my brother? And I am not a good son of the Emperor
Alexander, who, perhaps, will be the scourge of the Revolution? I
am not a son of the Emperor Alexander?”

In spite of the stentorian tone, the prince’s voice did not
sustain itself. He was poorly in health, and he had been used to
employing it to the maximum. He had no children, and, judging by his
tone, he seemed to doubt the existence of his son Vladimir, who was
not, it is true, to be seen, and yet he was Vladimir Mikhailovich
and his brother. But he was not a good son of the Emperor Alexander,
who was to be the scourge of the Revolution, or rather the scourge
of the Revolution, who was to annihilate the monster of the Revolution,
who was to rule the world, who was the scourge of the Revolution.

“Good heavens!” said Anna Pávlovna, and she smiled, which was
her usual expression when she was surprised. “You are a fool!”

The prince lifted his head, and, with the same stentorian voice,
again said:

“I am not a good son of the Emperor Alexander? I am not a good
son of the Emperor Alexander? I am not a good son of the Emperor
Alexander, who is to rule the world?”

“Don’t speak to me of the Emperor!” said Anna Pávlovna. “You are
a fool, a vulgar fool. Do you think that your father does not know
about your conduct? Your father knows everything. And you don’t even
know that. Your father always knows everything.”

“Go to the devil!” said the prince. “I don’t care about my
father.”

He had no more children, but he had a brother whom he despised and
from whom he had never received any happiness. He did not wish to
hear more about his brother, and he assured Anna Pávlovna that he
did not care about his father.

“Then why are you here?” said Anna Pávlovna, and she smiled.
“I thought you were going to get tea. I will make you a cup of
tea.”

“Perhaps you are right. I don’t see why I should not go and see
the Dowager Empress. I shall be glad to see her.”

“When you are done with her come and see me. I am very happy to
see you.”

And now, with a glance which suggested a mathematical equation, Anna
Pávlovna addressed herself to the tea. She was an actress, and the
conversational tableaux she played out were of the most varied
character. She was a courtier, an old woman, a protestant, a
full-blooded Russian. All these characters belonged to her and she
played them with equal assurance. Moreover, she was a Russian
woman, and, like all Russian women, she had a voice, which when it
did not sing was not at all unpleasant. She was also a woman of
worldly wisdom, and it would be hard to say whether this wisdom had
come from her head or her heart.

Prince Vasíli, who was not an old man, and who, judging from his
speech, was a man of the world, considered Anna Pávlovna to be a
coarse and vulgar woman. But this impression was a purely intellectual
one. Prince Vasíli was an artist, and in his eyes this woman, who
had been his friend for many years, was a woman of art, and he
admired her. Anna Pávlovna was not a woman of the world. She had never
tried to be a woman of the world, and she had never been successful.
At her reception, which was a great success, Prince Vasíli was the only
one who did not attend.

“I shall be very happy if your Highness will permit me to spend
the evening of the fete with you,” said the prince, rising from his
seat and bowing low, “but I am afraid I am not in a mood for
conversation.”

“Ah, you are ill! You don’t look well. Do you have a headache? I
presume?” said Anna Pávlovna, addressing the prince in her most
artless, womanly tone, and with the most flattering, intimate glance,
which the prince, though he was not a man of the world, could not
fail to notice. He bowed a little to signify that he had been
misunderstood, and placing his hand on her arm said:

“I am sorry, but I cannot stay with you. I have come to see you
because you have been ill, and because I care a great deal about you.
I should be sorry not to see you again.”

emphasis.

Anna Pávlovna Schérer had a right to be a favorite of the Empress,
for the Empress, who had a good memory and was an intelligent woman,
understood her, and knew that in the midst of her constant
enthusiasm there was always a certain reserve, which the Empress
appreciated and appreciated still more when she saw that Anna Pávlovna
was really tender-hearted and sincere.

only fond of Anna Pávlovna, but she was also a great admirer of her
poems. She had much sympathy with her; they were both good-hearted
women, and, though they differed in many respects, they were similar
in their veneration for the old and the new, the Russian and the
French. There was a time when Anna Pávlovna worked as a governess in
the Empress’s household. She wrote a number of charming little poems
for the Empress, and the Empress commended them to the attention of
the Imperial Academy of Sciences, of which she was a member, and
which, as everyone knows, is the highest court of appeal in the

literary journal, the Ópetich Dvóroz, and were admired by all
the literati of that time.

St. Petersburg, and she was so, because though she was an old and
fashionable woman, she was also, despite her age, extremely capable
and intelligent, and had a most pleasing manner.

evening.”

should I let you see me? You have come to see me, you are a good

we used to be.”

annoyed.

in a mood for the fete.”

The prince’s face was expressionless.

“It’s all I can do. Will you go out with me again?”

“Of course, I will go out.”

The prince bowed again and went out.

Anna Pávlovna was left alone wondering whether, as she had promised
the prince, she would see him again. She smiled; she was not in a
doubtful mood. When the prince was with her she was in a good mood,

he was a kind man.

Anna Pávlovna was a good woman. She had not the least idea of the
greatness of the man who came to see her. She had not even the least
idea that he was the prince of Russia.

Anna Pávlovna’s air of superiority was common to her whole family;
it was the result of her deep sense of her own beauty. Her face was
not beautiful, but her eyes were monitory and subjugating. She
possessed an irrefutable moral feeling and a sense of her own
importance, which made her look down upon the most eminent persons of
the world. She was a woman of letters and a great favorite of the Empress
Máriya Fëdorovna. Her manner of speaking was brusque, correct, and
cultivated, and she carried herself with the air of an artist. She
was a woman of rank and intelligence, and liked the Russians with whom
she lived, but in her society one could not be frivolous.

Prince Vasíli Kurágin smiled at her.

“Masha,” he said, “do you think it would amuse you to see the little
Cammerarius called an idiot? His little daughter has just been sent to
court. She is quite fascinating, and I should like to see her.”

“Who is this idiot?” asked Anna Pávlovna, making a great
effort to be trifling.

She had not been told of this little girl. She did not care to know
and would have been glad to be rid of the subject.

“I don’t know anyone by that name, but I think this is the mother of
your daughter. She is quite fascinating. Her voice is so musical. I
saw her here. I shall send you her card.”

“What a delightful person!” replied Anna Pávlovna. “In fact, I
have seen her before. Would you like her card? I shall be glad to give
it to you.”

“Your card, and what about others? You see, I must see them all.”

“You see, everyone wants to have your little daughter. I will give
you their cards. She is too pretty, too charming. I hope you will give
her some presents, for you cannot always give her money.”

“Does she have to wear the uniform?” asked the prince.

“Yes, she has to wear that uniform. She is going to the army. Maybe
she will hit the mark. But we ask nothing more than this from our
children. I hope she will go on and be a hero, like her father and
yourself, for my children are very beautiful and intelligent, but I
think they should be good, too, and have a beautiful destiny.”

Prince Vasíli did not answer, but bowed, signifying that he would
give the little girl some presents.

“Ah, yes,” said Anna Pávlovna, “you know, there is no one who
does not pay attention to that Cammerarius. She is so pretty, so
charming. But I don’t know whether they will allow her to enter
the army. Children must be so beautiful, so charming. But anyway,
I shall give you her card. It will amuse you very much to see
her. Adieu.”

Prince Vasíli Kurágin was delighted and a little perplexed. He
had expected an artistic creation, a great lady, a woman whose
word was law; intelligent, cultured, and refined, a favorite of His
Imperial Majesty. Anna Pávlovna Schérer had not been a lady at
all, though no one had ever noticed it. She was an old lady, a
character, an expert in the art of reading the signs of the times, but
not an artist. She was not a genius. She was no longer a woman of
letters, no longer a favorite of the Empress, and she was dying.

Anna Pávlovna was dying. It had been her habit to say to those who
knew her, that she had been “sent” to her grave by nature, and often
she thought of death. But she never had the notion of suicide
thought of by many women of her position. She died with her characteristic
resignation, but not with sadness. When she spoke of death, she
spoke of it with a smile. Notwithstanding her health, she spent her
time at the opera and in society, and despite her symptoms she did
what she had always done, received a great many friends, and talked
very much. On the day of her death she walked to the opera and arrived
at the theater a little after 10 in the evening. It was getting late,
as there were no lights, but a guest, not a friend, desired to see
her last performance, and Anna Pávlovna Schérer obliged him. She was
victorious in music and won the applause of the audience. She entered
the box on her usual sofa, where she lived, and she stroked her hand
with her hair, between her fingers, as if she still possessed the
power of life. Her hair was gray, and she was not even capable of
speaking. She died with a smile, and the smile on her face was
as if she had seen her death. But it was not a smile of triumph or
of satisfaction; it was a smile which only a woman capable of
amorousness could have worn. The smile was the smile of a woman who
loved, and who knew that she was dying.

WAS HE DEAD?

I.

During the past year the relations between the French and Russian
courts had not been satisfactory. French officers had addressed
impudent letters to the Empress Márya Fëdorovna, in which they
suggested that she disguise herself as the Empress’s daughter, and in
this way pass over into France, where she would aid the Emperor of
Russia with an army of 500,000 men. The number of Russian emigrants
living in Paris had increased daily, and beings unused to the
French language and customs had been trying their best to insult the
Russian women.

The Empress Márya Fëdorovna’s health had suffered and she had been
often taken ill; she had been murdered by influenza. She was a
woman of violent character and had not been able to bear without
anger the contempt with which the French, and particularly her
favorites, courtiers and enemies of Russia, had regarded her. She
had not, like those who had previously lived at the French court,
inherited an exquisite taste in matters of fashion; she had been
in the habit of wearing drab dresses, and had hated to be seen
in any other. She had been proud and jealous, and had ever been
capable of the most violent outbursts of passion.

She was no longer young, she was not happy. She was an old woman
with a strong character, who was only faithful in her passion to one
man. Her passion had been crushed. She had never been able to bear
that her favorite and her friend, Countess Razumovskaya, had accepted
the hand of the most odious man in Europe, Baron Funke. The Empress
had been ready to break off all relations with him, but the Countess
had interposed, and had offered to give up the baron. The Empress
had been furious, and she had tried all possible means to obtain
satisfaction.

The Countess Razumovskaya had been a favorite of the Empress since
her father’s death. A little girl she had long been the idol of the
Empress. She had sent her to school in Switzerland. She had brought her
up in the belief that she would become a lady, and she had received
all the scandalous attentions to which she was entitled. She was one
of the favorite victims of the Emperor’s enemies. Her father had been
barred from the Russian army. This Rastopchin had been one of the most
terrifying of all the enemies of the Emperor. She had been educated

The prince raised his eyebrows as she said he did not deserve to
have them, but answered:

“I don’t know what it is that makes my children so charming; I
know I don’t like them.”

“I don’t ask you to like them. That is not in your power,” replied
Anna Pávlovna with commiseration and with the tender smile which, as I
have said, expressed a perpetual consciousness of her charm. “What
bothers you, Prince?”

“I don’t know why I don’t like them,” said the prince. “But I
say to myself that children are the light of one’s life. I should
like them to be charming and adorable as my father-in-law is. Then
I should like to take them to the court, to the theater, to the balls,
and, my wife and I, to dine at the palace. I should like to pass
them off as my own grandchildren. But I cannot do that. I don’t know
why. I don’t like to see them.”

“Don’t live at the palace,” said Anna Pávlovna. “Live at the
Palace Corner. It is a fine house. And you could have a little
dining-room there, and then all your children would be proud to pass
you off as their grandfather.”

The prince sank into silence and looked at his hands as if they
were very painful to him. Anna Pávlovna continued:

“Emperor Alexander does not understand why you cannot live in the
palace. He thinks that if you did not live there it was because you
wanted to exercise your right to a private life. He thinks this is a
natural right. He would not understand if you would throw out your
children. He knows that you do not like them. He knows that you don’t
get along with them. He knows that they are insolent and some of them
have grown too old. But he knows that you would never do so. He
thinks that this is a natural right of your children. And he
wouldn’t understand if you threw them out of your family.”

“I don’t like to see them,” said the prince. “I don’t know why.”

“God knows,” said Anna Pávlovna. “Princes and emperors know why.”

The prince began to laugh in the usual tipsy manner of his. He
had a bad temper, and being neither sober nor of a taciturn nature,
this was a favorite way of his of expressing himself.

“A grandiose idea! Ah, grandiose! I believe that my children have
the gift of natural melody and harmony, and therefore I don’t
like them. And emperors don’t understand. I believe that a man
must have a talent, must feel a duty, must be a genius and be
humiliated in order to live, and I think that nature has given
them that gift. And I think that a man who is a genius is a
genius only with respect to those around him. The greatest
geniuses are those who are humblest. If there were no emperors
I could not be a genius. I should be a perfect dunce.”

“Don’t live at the palace!” insisted Anna Pávlovna. “And you
must give me your daughter’s hand. You know it is my intention to
speak to the Emperor to-morrow.”

The prince, who was in the habit of offending her by saying
“yes” and “no” at the same time, said:

“Anna Pávlovna, please don’t remind me of my daughter. If you
suggest it, I will be angry.”

“I shall not do that. It is my duty. No, do not be angry. You
have been our friend for so long. Do not speak to me of your
daughter’s hand. It is suggested, that is all.”

“Don’t tease me. I don’t want to speak of my daughter this
evening. I am not in a humor. It is not her fault. I am tired.”

Anna Pávlovna sat down to the fireplace, and the prince moved
to the table.

“Now is the time,” said he, “to ask you, dear Anna Pávlovna,
for the hand of your mother-in-law’s first cousin, the baroness
Vasília Mikhailowna Scherkoff, who is engaged to my son Prince
Pavel. You know that she is a divine creature. I must have her.”

“Nonsense! I don’t know this baroness. I have not seen her in years.
I have been ill for some days. But perhaps you don’t know her. I
didn’t know poor Zarreyka’s cousin, the baroness Trepova, until her
death.”

“Anna Pávlovna, please don’t tease me. I don’t want to speak
of my daughter’s hand. I am not in a humor.”

“Be not angry. You will not be angry. But this baroness
Scherkoff is not the person for you. She is not even your
daughter’s cousin. She is not the same person as her mother. And
I am only of second cousins with her—a very remote relative.
You do not know her. Forgive me, I am very sorry.”

“You will be sorry all your life. I know that it was your
mother-in-law who married her to the baron. But you have not
seen her.”

“Then you don’t know her,” replied the prince, “I don’t know
her.”

“Nonsense.”

“I am tired.”

Anna Pávlovna rose and sat down on the sofa, and the prince went
to the table. After some time she said:

“Would you like a cup of coffee or tea?”

“I don’t know that I am tired”—said the prince. “I think
I am quite full of life. I am very well. I am tired only when
my brain is not at work.”

Anna Pávlovna remained silent. After a long pause she said:

“Prince Felix of the Netherlands did not like his children. And
a great king who is the son of a great king, a great man, a
great statesman, a man of genius, with a lofty and self-abnegating soul,
who, at his age, is crowned with laurels, and who is expected to
conquer the world, does not like his children. I think that is a
sign of something.”

“You are not well. I will go.”

“Be not angry. I am only talking nonsense. I lost my mother,
the Countess Lukomskay, when I was only fifteen. I don’t know
why I am so insolent and proud, so rude and ungrateful to my
father, the Count Pavel Lukomsky, and I think that a man should
be grateful to his father for everything he has. I don’t know
why I should not be grateful to my parents for their own
children. But I am ungrateful. And my mother-in-law is very
old and very unwell. And my children are so charming. And
I don’t like them. And that is a sign of something. I don’t
know what.”

Anna Pávlovna, to whom a wounded pride could not stand the pain of
conflict, and who, in spite of her knowledge of the prince, was led
into an excrescence by his oddities, said:

“I think that perhaps you are the son of a duchess. Perhaps your
mother is a duchess, and you are called to the court as a punishment
for your mother’s high birth. And perhaps you are unhappy because
your mother is not there. Perhaps she is unhappy. You may have
scorned her, you may have insulted her in your youth. Perhaps she
is waiting for you. Perhaps she is a duchess. Perhaps you are
a son of a duchess. And you are not unhappy. She disappears,
but only your own children remain. And she is dead. And you
have no pity for your children and you don’t want to live with
them. And perhaps this is a sign of something. Perhaps you are
unhappy, perhaps you are not. It is all I know. I do not know
why.”

She looked at the prince with a half smiling, half reproaching
expression. The prince did not know whether to laugh or to tell her
that he had not come to see her to talk about his children.

“All this is nonsense,” he said. “I want to be alone.”

“I think the life of a Prince is very hard, but I think that if
your children did not exist you would be happy. You would be
happy if you had no children. You are not in love with your
children. You don’t love them. And you know yourself that you
do not want them, and you will keep them, because they are in
your power, and you would like to pass them off as your own
children.”

“You are a charming woman, dear Anna Pávlovna, and I am very
grateful. I think that if I had been represented by your
mother-in-law as an old woman in the manner of the Courtier
who had presented himself to her and had evinced his respect
for her age, I should have been pleased to see her. I don’t
think that it was such an unworthy, ungrateful creature as
you, Lady Anna Pávlovna, who is my son-in-law. You would
have been a perfect woman, among whom Horace says that a man
sought for a wife. I think you are like the Greek woman, whom
Plato says, although he speaks of her only in the plural form,
that a man should seek for a wife. But I am only a lucky
chance.”

Anne Pávlovna, to whom this seemed a pleasant answer, and perhaps
not altogether insincere, told the prince that she was going to
her lodging to take a siesta.

“Don’t wait for me. I will call you tomorrow. I have some
business to attend to. I am the son of a duchess.”

“Come,” said Anna Pávlovna as she took her bonnet from the
chair, “I will give you this bonnet. It is rather old. It
is not the kind of bonnet that the Princess would give you.
But I thought perhaps it might be a little useful to you.”

“Thank you, thank you. I am a lucky chance.”

“Come, I will give you this bonnet.”

Prince Vasíli came away shaking his hands. He was calm, dignified,
and spoke with the gentleness of a great man whose tone was never
interrupted by laughter.

“God bless you. I am a lucky chance. I am an old woman.”

“Come,” insisted Anna Pávlovna, “and I will give you this
bonnet.”

The prince came up to her. He was sorry to go. He had not come to
see her to talk about his children. But he knew that she would not
let him off.

“I am a lucky chance. I am an old woman.”

“Come,” insisted Anna Pávlovna, “I will give you this
bonnet.”

After he had gone, Anna Pávlovna remained sitting at the
fireplace, pondering over what he had said. She was a rather
unusual human being. She was a very old woman—she was forty years
old. She was a woman of great education, of a most refined
society, and she knew the first beginnings of political movements
in Europe. But she was a woman of average intelligence, and the
admiration of the courtiers, a great lady, who, she said herself,
was repulsed by her insignificance, and who had been there, a
young girl, in the time of Catherine the Great, was her only
return. She was the daughter of a natural, and perhaps illegitimate
son of the Countess Lukomskaya, who was then a lady-in-waiting
at the court of Catherine the Great. He afterward married a
nobleman’s daughter.

The Countess Lukomskaya was an original, a woman whose character was
adored by the courtiers, and whom the Empress fought to make a
countess, but which could not be done because of her origin. The
Countess Lukomskaya was famous for her large reputation, her
exquisite taste, her elegant manners, her love of children, and
her maternal devotion to her children. She was, from the day
she was born, often ill, and then her face was covered with
precious stones, her hands were enclosed in lace, and a lace
bonnet on her head looked like powder. She was buried in the

The prince smiled and said:

“Anatole is the most charming child who can be born. What a beautiful
character! How much I have learned from him! I think I could never
have learned better if I had studied philosophy.”

“I haven’t been able to study it myself, but I have heard a great
deal of it.”

Anna Pávlovna said this with a smile, as if unable to restrain herself
from expressing her admiration for the Prince’s son.

“I am so ashamed to confess it,” he continued, looking at Anna
Pávlovna with a sound of genuine emotion in his voice, “I am ashamed
to admit it, but my eldest daughter is so disinterested that I am
ashamed to protect her. She is so chaste, so innocent. It seems to me
that if she were to enter a convent, it would be all right.”

Anna Pávlovna said nothing. The prince looked at her earnestly, and
she answered not a word. At times the prince was overbearing, even to
the point of rudeness, in his high opinion of himself and of others, but
he is not a man who can reveal his feelings. In his magnificent and
overbearing air, in his refined manners, and in his brilliant
conversation, in his polished surface, he hides an ardent and gloomy
soul. He does not like to be reproached even for the slightest thing,
and it would take a great deal to make him admit his faults. And
therefore he is silent when one tries to make him acknowledge them.

But Anna Pávlovna had the narrow and proud Russian mind, which does
not tolerate, nor even permit, the slightest impropriety. She looked
at the prince and, with the reserve and reserve of her native spirit,
impartially reproached him, reproached him with infinite blandness and
sweetness, and he smiled in thought.

“I am so grateful to you for your attentions, dear friend,” said the
prince in the same low tone, this time even more earnestly; “you have
the most charming and noble heart.”

The prince again fixed his eyes on Anna Pávlovna, smiling, and
suspected that she might soon reproach him for those same attentions.
She smiled back and said:

“I have never had any heart to reproach you for, for you are
the most charming cultivator of women.”

“Ah, if you only knew.”

“Who? Me?” said Anna Pávlovna, with the sudden impulse and
simplicity of her spirit, laughing at the prince. “Ah, I see now! It
is not I. And what is it you yearn for?”

“Come, just name your dear Prince.”

“I am nervous about that. But I have a daughter who will be thirty
years old in a few weeks, and I don’t want to lose her.”

“Do you want to lose her?” said Anna Pávlovna with a laugh. “I
have a daughter who will be twenty years old in two months, and I
am as happy as you are.”

“Poor child! Well, keep her.”

“I don’t know the customs of my country,” the prince said with
an air of regret; “though I am an old Prussian I am not at all
used to the idea of marriage. I have a daughter to protect.”

In these words he imitated the English. As a matter of fact, the
prince had no intention of marrying his daughter, but he was afraid of
receiving reproaches, and he found it impossible to say the truth. He
was in the habit of talking nonsense in order to hide his real
sentiments.

He looked earnestly at Anna Pávlovna who smiled at him.

“I have been thinking,” he said, “that though I am a foreigner
I am very Russian in my heart, so much so that I am quite a
Russian.”

“This is a very fine thing to say,” said Anna Pávlovna. “You
have to exert yourself to show that you are a prince.”

At this point the conversation, as is natural, changed. The prince
shut his eyes, and the conversation, which had not before had an
individual character, assumed a role and became a dialogue. It was
comical and these comical moments were for the prince the best
moments of the evening. He had always liked comical things when he was
alone, and now he played the part of the comic, like an actor, and he
and Anna Pávlovna acted the comedy.

“I have a daughter to protect,” said the prince again. “That
daughter is so charming. If she were to marry well now, she would be
quite a success; but if she remains unmarried for a month and a half,
she becomes tragic.”

“She does not have to marry,” said Anna Pávlovna. “All the same,
you must protect her. If she marries poorly, you must protect her.”

“I have never thought of that. She is my own daughter.”

“Who have you been thinking of?” said Anna Pávlovna. “Your
nephew’s son or your niece’s son? Oh! I have the most charming
nephew’s son.”

“Who?” asked the prince.

“Prince Saltykov. He has just returned from his tour. He is
the most charming youth in St. Petersburg.”

“I don’t know this Prince Saltykov,” said the prince.

“I have heard,” said Anna Pávlovna. “Triumphal return from
the tour. Men travel and women do not.”

“I have always thought,” said the prince, “that if a man were to
put his head in the clouds and think, there would not be any need
to consult a doctor; he would get a bit of the same as women do.”

The two laughed.

“Sometimes,” continued the prince, “there seems to me to be a vast
difference between a prince and a general. A prince is neither
a fool nor a miser, but a general is either a fool or a miser.
How do you think a general is? Um! Um! I don’t think there
can be a better general than the Emperor Alexander himself.
I believe the Emperor Alexander will end by marrying either
or none, and that will be a good thing. I think the Emperor
Alexander will marry two of his sons. I think he will marry
them both to his own children.”

“I think nothing,” said the prince, “of anything. I think
my daughter will be married soon. I am afraid she will be
married soon.”

As it was now 10 o’clock, the prince rose to go.

“I must be going,” said he, “I have much to do. I have been
younger than this. I have seen many things and I am no longer
young. I must be going.”

“Come,” said Anna Pávlovna, “let us adjourn the discussion
of my nephew’s son to another time. Come, let me find out whether
you have a taste for French variety show. I am changing my
dress. Let us adjourn the discussion of my nephew’s son,
and I shall be more than glad to see you.”

“I am glad. I am glad,” said the prince.

The prince was the last to go, and he sat down next to Anna Pávlovna.
He had an unerring instinct about Anna Pávlovna’s attitude toward
relations between the sexes. If she liked him, he did not pay her
attention, but if she did not, he followed her.

Anna Pávlovna led the way to a room where the prince sat down after a
momentary hesitation. The prince was always courteous and lady-like
toward women, but he never crossed a line.

As he sat down, the prince said to Anna Pávlovna:

“Come, give me your hand. I have been dreaming.”

“I am not sure that I may give you my hand.”

“Why not?”

“As you are a foreigner.”

“Why?”

“Because, you know, there are some things you must not do, like a
prince.”

“Ah!” said the prince. “We must not do some things to each other.
What things?”

“When you are here, we do not do everything to each other.”

“You are a very charming young woman. You have a charming smile,
and a charming way of looking.”

“I am a charming young woman,” said Anna Pávlovna. “I am a
charming young woman.”

“And why not?”

“I am a charming young woman.”

“May I kiss your hand? I really do not know how to behave.”

Anna Pávlovna smiled, and at the same time said:

“Come, just take my hand.”

The prince said nothing, but there came a smile to his lips as he
kissed Anna Pávlovna’s hand.

“You don’t speak. I think you are ashamed of your pride. I have
always thought you a very proud man. I think you are ashamed
of your pride. But it is a charming pride.”

“I am very ashamed,” said the prince, smiling.

“Come, you shouldn’t be ashamed. Take my hand.”

The prince took Anna Pávlovna’s hand, and while she was looking
at him, he smiled.

“I think,” said Anna Pávlovna, “that the whole world is now
watching you.”

“Do you think?” said the prince.

“You must be very careful. It is all very serious. You should
not be ashamed of your pride. It is a charming pride.”

“The whole world is watching me,” said the prince. “Yes, it is
all very serious. It is all very serious.”

“Will you leave me alone? I have been waiting for you all evening.”

“I can’t, I can’t.”

“Come, I will give you a place. I am trying to tell you some
things.”

“Only if I am going to talk a little, and you are going to listen.”

“I have been waiting for you all evening.”

“I can’t,” said the prince. “Can we go somewhere?”

“I will give you a place.”

“Let us go to the library. Do you think they would like to see
you?”

“I don’t think they would like to see me.”

“Let us go to my house. Let us. I shall be glad to see you there.”

“I don’t know.”

“I think it would be much better. I shall be glad to see you
there. I shall give you a place.”

“I can’t.”

“Let us go to the library. Your house is too far. Do you think
they would like to see you there?”

“I don’t think they would like to see me.”

“I don’t know, I don’t know.”

“I have been waiting for you all evening.”

“Can we go somewhere?”

“I shall be glad to see you there. I shall give you a place.”

“I don’t know.”

The prince looked at Anna Pávlovna. Her eyes were fixed on him. He
smiled. The prince was tall and handsome, with a high, flat, and
smooth forehead. He wore a court uniform which was too small for him,
and this, together with his amiable smile, gave him an impression of
power.

The prince seemed to be sorry that the time had come for him to leave
St. Petersburg and to return to Germany. He was restless in his
conversation and he made more efforts to subdue his emotions in order
to conceal them. He continually caught the eye of Anna Pávlovna and
smiled. His reason for wishing to conceal his emotions was that he
could not bear to see Anna Pávlovna grow angry with him. She was all
power to him; she was the only one who could influence him, and he
was afraid to make her angry. He was afraid, and he hated to be
afraid; and he hated and could not bear the thought that when he returned
to Germany he would be unable to subdue his passion for Anna Pávlovna.

He, the prince, careerist and explorer, felt himself frustrated and
shamed. He was ashamed and furious. He could not bear it, and he could
not understand it. He, a man expecting to be a great soldier, and
an explorer, could not understand why he made no effort to master the
femme fatale. He, the prince, was in a state of which he knew nothing,
and he did not know why he was unable to subdue this passion. He
wanted to be a great soldier, and to be an explorer, and he did not
understand the secret meaning of his life and could not believe that
he was not a great man. But he did not understand that he was in love
with Anna Pávlovna and that he was bound to feel a profound and painful
inefficiency, inasmuch as he was unable to master her. In this moment
of weakness he felt himself a failure, and he did not understand how he
had once imagined that he might become a great man. He wanted to be a
great soldier, and he saw himself mingling with the French and Russian
generals at the Battle of Eylau, as he had long ago imagined he would
do if he were a great man. He would go to the front as a great man and
be a great soldier. He could not comprehend that he had given himself
over to Anna Pávlovna Schérer, and he did not understand why in spite
of his desires he could not subdue her passion. He would like to be a
great man, but he was unable to subdue his passion. He would like to be
an explorer and he was afraid of the unknown. He would like to be a
great man, and he did not understand his own weakness. He was ashamed
and furious and he could not understand why he could not subdue Anna
Pávlovna. It was impossible for him to believe that she was capable of
making him suffer. He could not understand the cause of his weakness.
He made no effort to conquer her and he hated himself for it.

Pávlovna, but was simply the result of her being unable to resist
the prince, gave a very clear idea of the man’s character, and served
as a kind of confession of his inner life. It will be of interest to
read it to the reader, and the reader will be able to judge for himself
whether Anna Pávlovna was not right in saying that the whole world was
watching the prince.

“You are bestial,” she added in a tone on which he could not
disagree. “Selfish! Perhaps you feel, like your father, the same
feelings toward your children as you have toward your so-called
‘friends,’ people you do not like but who depend on you. In truth,
why do you say that you love these people?”

The prince, taking a napkin, wiped his mouth. He had always been
frightened of his wife. She was so energetic, even when she was ill
and weak. He was a highly educated man, but he was old, almost a
century, and had just lost his wife. He had become so energetic,
independent, and even active that once he had had to put her into a
chair to enable her to come and go with ease. He had yet to add
to this that he was the eldest son of the Church, the president of
the Christian High Council, the last surviving member of the old
Russian aristocracy, and that he still possessed many properties and
a great fortune. But he no longer regretted that he was old and
weakened, that he could not dance. On the contrary, he enjoyed this
change. What an honor to be allowed to talk to himself and to
the people he loved, and not to dance! But he was a very exacting
and fastidious person, and this fine and ancient Russian aristocrat,
who for many years had been involved in the highest circles, was
particularly irritated by those who, confusing the ice with the water,
did not observe the differences between the different classes of
Russian society. He wanted to be an old lady, an elderly lady of
the court. He had not changed, but he had become younger, and he
dared to think that he was even richer than he had been. At the
same time, however, he had to admit that he was a great hypocrite,
that his court manners, which hitherto had always served to separate
him from the common folk and to conceal from them the real cause of
his dislike for them, were now being used to deceive them.

Such were the thoughts that passed through the mind of Prince Vasíli
Kurágin as Anna Pávlovna Schérer went on talking.

“You have been a great hypocrite,” she continued, “and you will
become one still more. You have become even better than your father,
who was so spiteful. He would have broken the neck of the first man
who dared give his daughter to the first man who did not stand well
with him. He would have done this even more than he did when his
nobility finally proclaimed itself, by the way, of which you showed
no sign. You do not have the vulgarity of the old aristocracy, which
never cared what its son was going to be and which did not mind if
the son married whoever he chose to marry. But you like to marry
people of your own caste, and openly.”

The prince maintained his silence. Anna Pávlovna continued in her
usual style of conversation.

“Do you know? Of course you do know that the dowager Empress Márya
Fëdorovna has decided to let out a great ball. Why not? It is a
delight. The Empress herself will attend it in order to show that it
is no ordinary affair. She is attending. February is the month of the
Empress Márya Fëdorovna’s balls. But the Empress herself will always
come. I know that she will come. The Empress has decided to go
to the ball and stay there till the end. We are going to have a
great evening. There will be so many people. We will dance till the
very end.”

“When the ball is over,” said the prince, in his usual cold,
conversational style, “I will go to the English ambassador’s.”

Anna Pávlovna gave a little laugh.

“It is not the habit of the Empress to go to the English
ambassador’s,” she said.

“Very good,” replied the prince, “but it is the habit of the
Russian ambassador to go to the balls, and that is in Kiev.”

Though the prince’s manner indicated that he was pleased he had
said something which he really did not say, Anna Pávlovna shuddered
at his words.

“I shall not go to the ball,” replied the prince. “I shall not
go. Life is hard for old people.”

“I think it is hard for all of us,” retorted Anna Pávlovna. “I am
going to the ball. I shall go. I shall go all the way with your
daughter. You will come too, and we shall dance as we used to do.
Dance, dance! It will be interesting. You know one of our great
friends, Countess Krasnovskaya, is getting ready to go to St. Petersburg
for the winter. She is even more charming than she was before. How
charming! When do you expect her?”

“Tomorrow,” said the prince.

“Tomorrow? Oh, when is she coming? Do you mean to say she comes
so soon? Yes, she is so charming. Some people say she does not
really know how to dance....”

The prince grew silent.

“I only wish that foreigners might learn to dance as they used
to. They all seem to have forgotten the old-time court dances....
I do not know. One never sees the people who used to dance at court.
Perhaps the new dancers will have the same faults as the old ones.”

“The new dancers are much cleverer than the old ones. The old
ones were too clever,” said the prince, in his usual self-satisfied
tone.

“And they did not know how to dance. But at court, at the court
ballet, everyone was as stupid as a donkey. Some people say that
Krasnovskaya is not so big as her sister. Do not you know that
she is much smaller than her sister? Do you know it? I shall go
to the ball. I shall go with your daughter. It will be a great
dinner. I shall go with your daughter to show my loyalty to the
Empress.”

“You know,” said the Prince Vasíli, “I have always thought that
there was a certain resemblance between Krasnovskaya and her aunt.”

“Do you mean the favorite aunt? The Empress will be very glad
to see her aunt from the court of Russia, who is not of the same
court, and to see her aunt from the court of the King of Prussia.

loves to see all the courts of Europe. This is the only reason
why it is so necessary that the court of Russia should be
represented and that all ambassadors should be on her list of
entertainments.”

“Do I? I don’t understand you. You are always so nice!” replied the
prince in his most affected tone. “If you would only have some tact,
you would never say such things.”

“I sincerely wish that were so,” replied Anna Pávlovna. “Then you
would be happy. Then you would be happy if you were to hear what
Humbert said when he was here. He would joyfully acknowledge that it is
true, that he has a beautiful son, an heir to the throne. But, eh
well! I must say that the poor boy is very unhappy. He does not know
what to do with such a gift. He is unhappy because he is poor
and has no connections; he is unhappy because his father has
abandoned him. Oh, the children are happy and insane with joy! ... The
poor boy, how I pity him! The poor boy, when I see him I think of my
daughter and her child. She was a great step forward, despite her
extravagances.... It is a pity, really a pity, to compare one child to
another. There is a great world in that unhappy family of yours. God
knows what is going on behind closed doors. Let me say I have a good
opinion of your eldest, the Baroness von Lawo. She is a clever girl.
She leaves nothing to be desired. She is a remarkable chief of staff in
the Duchy of Hesse. That won’t be finished yet. The Duchess is a
dainty creature. She is fond of her children. She is a joyous creature,
a lovely creature. They say she is fond of the Emperor Alexander, and
it’s a pity, but it’s a pity it won’t be so for long. She is to
return to her husband’s service, to pass the winter in Trier. You have
your cousin’s head on a pin, you can always come to her. And then, if
you will, come to see me. I shall be charmed to see you.”

The prince, as usual, did not trouble to answer, but remained silent.
Thus, with invariable politeness and a smile, Anna Pávlovna did what
she had not intended to do, getting the prince to admit, without
knowing it, that he was jealous of his son.

“May I introduce the Vicomte de Mortemart?” said the speaker in
mid-conversation.  

Prince Vasíli, who had risen as if in a hurry, thought it proper
to pay his respects to the Vicomte, who bowed to him, and then
passing the sick Anna Pávlovna to a chair, he said to the prince, with
a drawing of his lips, that he, the Vicomte, had come from Marseilles
just in time to see the Young Napoleon, who was on his knees before
him, begging for a drop of water. He had not seen this since the
Battle of Marengo and he was not to be satisfied with half-measures;
he wanted to see the Prince Impérial as he was. He had approached the
boy like a father and guided him to a chair, and the young emperor
sat on the knees of the Vicomte, who with a short exclamation of
amazement asked the Vicomte of Mortemart, who had been weeping, how
anyone could have seen such a scene.

“It is not the first time,” said the Vicomte. “I have often seen
the Prince Impérial weeping, and basing my life on my devotion to
the Buonaparte dynasty, I can, and will continue to, do my utmost to
support my dear sovereign, whose existence is the first thing in my
life. And a man likes to serve his sovereign in the only way he knows
how, and the only way he knows how is that of a father.”

The prince had risen again and had bowed to the Vicomte, saying he
was a most interesting man.

“I have no idea,” said the Vicomte, “that you do not know our
friend and brother, the Abbé Morio. Do you know him?”

“No,” replied the prince.

The Vicomte continued:

“I have not seen him in fifteen years. The last time I saw him the
Abbé was a cripple. I saw him lying on a mat in a small room, with
his arms in wheelchairs, and his head on a pillow. Everything was
in ruins and desolation. They said he had the vitiligo, but I saw
him myself. His mother had been sent to a convent, and he was there
too. I had no time to stop him from saying it was true, for there was
a dragoon soldier there, and I didn’t want him to say it. I was
very glad to see him, and I wanted to see him again. I was glad to see
him again, but the Abbé Morio was a cripple and only his eyes were
normal. I wanted to see him again, but today I didn’t find him. He
has left London.”

Anna Pávlovna, who, forgetting that she was suffering from la grippe,
had risen, and wished to say something to the Vicomte, bit her lip and
found nothing to say.

“I was here,” said Prince Vasíli, “to hear what you have to say
about the Baron Funke. I have been here for a long time.”

“To say what? Nothing. But that does not mean anything. I am waiting
for the Dowager Empress.”

The prince, getting up, bowed to the Vicomte, who had risen too, and
said:

“I am leaving. I have rejoined my wife. I wish you good health.”

The Prince of Hohenlohe had been waiting a long time in the
Empress’s pavilion. He had wished to obtain an audience with her since
the announcement of the dispatch of Novosíltsev, but the Empress had
been indisposed. He had been summoned by the Empress’s sister, the
Dowager Empress Márya Fëdorovna, and asked to come and tell her all
the news. She wanted to know how the whole army was getting along.
The Prince had not yet told her that Novosíltsev’s dispatch had
been burned and that he was ready to burn his own boats.

The Dowager Empress had received with marked interest the Austrian
admiral, Count Migl, who had been sent from Vienna to inform her that
the Emperor had accepted a post in the British service, that he was
in London, and also to tell her that the treaty of neutrality had
been concluded between Vienna and Paris. She had also received a
report from Wellington that he had not received any news as to the
proceedings of the Russian troops.

The Prince of Hohenlohe, seeing the Dowager Empress Márya Fëdorovna
in her pavilion, said, “I brought the dispatch. It’s ready.”

She took the dispatch with a somewhat shaken hand, and said:

“Well, how are the troops? What news do you bring me?”

The prince did not know what to reply. He did not wish to tell her
what the Emperor Alexander had decided, and she was entitled to know
it, and a man’s reserve and discretion were not enough to prevent her

flag in the French port of Brest will be rescued by the Flemings.”

the Dowager Empress.”

“Her Majesty is completely correct,” said Prince Vasíli, adding with
yawning irony: “Poor woman! I don’t believe that the signing will
happen. And as for the Flemings I know that they will not do a thing.
They are not Leghieuxs, they are only Flemings. But, I suppose as a
moral certainty, the things promised will be done. I think we are
closer to a divorce than anything else.”

“Then! Then we will be free again!” cried Anna Pávlovna, laughing
exuberantly, and the prince smiled.

“I repent of my innuendoes,” he said. “But, Anna Pávlovna, you are
getting too old for all this romance.”

“It is true.”

“You think so?” asked the prince.

“Yes,” replied Anna Pávlovna. “It is true.”

“All these affairs! My dear friend, why worry about these superficial
things?”

“But the diversion is very pleasant,” replied Anna Pávlovna. “I
imagine I have said much that you do not believe. I do not wish to
bother you. I imagine you now have a very pleasant evening. I will not
be surprised if you are up late. You must be tired. Will you think of
us tonight? I will not connect my ideas with yours in any way. As
for me, I am a lonely woman. I am not married. And then I have the
misfortune to speak freely. Come, let us raise a glass to the great
Emperor, and to the Empress, and to the illustrious Empress Dowager.”

Prince Vasíli raised his glass and said, with a commanding, imperious
emphatic intonation:

“A magnificent example!”

Yes, the Russian language was a noble language. The Empress Dowager,
who had so much power, so much influence and prestige with the Russian
Emperor, who sat entirely on the bosom of the monarch, was, she
believed, magnificently given to the poor and to the powerful, and had
no other aim in life than to please and be obeyed by the Emperor.

The prince went indoors after a glass of spirituous liquor, and Anna
Pávlovna Schérer, who was already coughing violently, sat down by a
grand piano, and started tenderly playing arias of Rossini.

While she was playing the prince approached another piano and, as he
thanked the musician she played for him, he began to whistle a
formidable fanfare. He had always taken a pleasure in instrumentally
mocking one of the Empress’s favorites, the dowager, who played
violins, and who preferred swallowing the fruits of Venus to the music
of Mozart. The prince kept on whistling, and the lamp in the room blew
out, and finally he went to bed.

Prince Vasíli was a man of eighty-four years and, although he was
the first of his ancestors to emigrate in a chest of drawers, he
retained by nature all the qualities which were the privilege of
his family. He had on his hands and feet signs of the rack, and his
speech was that of another time and another court. He used the dusty
and worn expressions of the old, weary nobility, the balloons of which
had burst, but whose continued existence was due to the fortunate
circumstance that they were tolerated by the sovereign who recognized
him as a representative of the nation, but who paid no heed to him
as a person.

His great-grandfather, as well as his grandfather, was a favorite of
the monarchs. His ancestor, Grand Duke Yelé Arévalovitch Romanoff, and
his three uncles were all at the same time. They used to waste away
at the court, as dog-heads guided sedately by clergy, dressed in tight
bodices and riding with two aides-de-camp—a fact not in the least
palpable to their two aides-de-camp, but ever perceptible to their
family host. They constantly offered their services to the Czar, who
listened to them coldly, with the eyes fixed on their icy boots.

His father had been in the Imperial Guard and his mother was a Polish
countess who did not know how to please, but who tried cleverly to
serve her husband. A deep hatred linked her in life with the czarist
family. He, therefore, had sacrificed his parents to his ambitious sons
and sons-in-law. He had been the first to take Anatole to the
court, declaring that he was an aristocrat and connected with the
lowest class of the nobility. The ambassador saw a little on his prince
at the court of Russia. The ambassador was a Frenchman and very
impatient like (he thought) his daughter-in-law, but it was not long
before he began to growl at her that she was a French parlant, and
that she was neither French nor beautiful. The ambassador knew the
prince, for his father—Grand Duke Nikolai Nikolaévitch Romanoff,
the Russian grand duke—had known him well, and the ambassador, besides
being a diplomat, was also a soldier and heavy driver. Grand Duke
Nikolai Nikolaévitch tended to believe that his wife was a native of
Bohemia, though she really was a Polish countess. The count herself
inherited from her ancestors a sense of humor and great cunning, and
kept up a most amusing correspondence with a grand duke who was not
only not a Russian, but quite the reverse, and who, at least in
appearance and in his mental attitude, was nice enough.

Grand Duke Nikolai Nikolaévitch Romanoff, it is important to say, was
not a Russian. He was an aristocrat, a bibliomaniac, and very much
attached to his parents, whom he adored. His daughter, his only son,
and other relatives were all very dear to him. The only person he did
not like was his wife, whose plain face, big dark eyes, and Mongoloid
features he hated.

He was also a tender skier. He possessed the right of first choice
on the ceremonial of the Grand Duke Court. He was a cross between
Boris Godunov and Paul the First.

Grand Duke Nikolai Nikolaévitch Romanoff, whose interest was
exclusively in his family, loved Socrates, Xenophon, and Plato, and
dedicated himself with great ardor to a very ancient philosophy. He
was an eloquent statesman, a true philosopher. He had, despite his
late appearance, a mind of great breadth, and a legalistic cast of
judgment.

He, with the rest of his family, loved his paternal grandmother,
Grand Duchess Maria Pavlovna, also a Russian but a royal. She had often
told him the blackest stories about the Empress, that was her brother’s
wife, the Dowager Empress. Grand Duke Nikolai Nikolaévitch was very
astonished to find that his relatives were not able to find fault with
the Dowager Empress. She never addressed him; he addressed her with
courtesy. His mother; his wife (his father was dead); his sister-in-law
(Princess Gorcekova, the sister of the Dowager Empress), whom Grand
Duke Nikolai Nikolaévitch loved; his daughter; his son by his wife—his
only son—his other daughter; his mother and father, whom he loved, so
that the sum of his family was unusually great, and, to sum up, it
included the Bogorodtchinsky Cathedral, which he had entirely built with
his own hands at the expense of the emperors.

He was exceptionally intelligent, and had accepted the name of
Vasílievitch. He was among those who used the oldest form of address
in common with their father and siblings. To Grand Duke Nikolai
Nikolaévitch Romanoff, the Emperor could be called at once with
respect and acquaintance. It was a privilege for Grand Duke Nikolai
Nikolaévitch, who always said “Your Majesty” to all his subjects, and
“your Majesty” to all his family, to abandon this general rule and to
call the Emperor “your majesty” for his benefit and to himself.

These Russians, who, in the eighteenth century, were not at all
unlike the French aristocracy of the time, were destined to play a very
important role in the life of the Russian court and to secure a certain
place in the Russian pantheon.

These were the people who cultivated the Romanoff dynasty as a hobby;
and the fact that Grand Duke Nikolai Nikolaévitch Romanoff was a
bibliomaniac and an artist of the most irritable temper, a man who took
eternal vengeance on enemies of his family who insulted even his very
name, and that his language was always a pious one, in which he used
the most ingenuous expressions when he could, while at the same time he
refused to understand anything that did not perfectly correspond to his
notion of a family, had nothing to do with his life, and indicated his
ignorance or vice, and finally the fact that he was, by a curious
coincidence, entirely one of a kind with the Empress, who was born a
princess in the neighborly traditions of the Russian monarchy, had
everything to do with his misfortune.

Grand Duke Nikolai Nikolaévitch had been at the court of Russia, and
in his family the Romanoffs had kept up the traditions of the old
dynasty; Grand Duchesses, who could not agree with their mothers, having
become the wives of the French, the Dutch, and even the Swiss
emperors, had one class in common: the uncles—“the mothers’ uncles,”
as Minzina was pleased to say—that were brought up at the Romanoff
court. The Russian grand dukes, who were the husbands of the French,
Dutch, and Swiss empresses, soon in the presence of the three great
husbands of their female relatives received a very unromantic and
unmusical name—which, it may be added without exaggeration, gave
imaginary authority to their advice or even to their very words: the
Rohans or the Soubrys, who were, however, all wisps of foam.

The grandfather of Grand Duke Vasíli Kurágin, who died young, was
known as the Duc d’Argentan; and Grand Duke Vassili Kolokoltsovitch
Romanoff, the father of Prince Vasíli himself, who was a favorite
vassal of the Czar Anton I Petróvitch, belonged to the Soubry family.
Grand Duke Vasíli and his father, according to the fashionable French
form of address, were called M. de Soubry, and the Duc d’Argentan
was, as he could readily show, the last of the Soubrys.

Grand Duke Vassili Kurágin was always respectful but not reverent
towards the Empress, the daughter of his great-grandmother, a pure
Romanoff. He had little knowledge of her life, but he always hesitated
in addressing her, thinking that her father (the Empress’s grandfather,
who had married his ill-fated grandmother, the aforesaid Empress, who
reigned under the name of Empress Maria Fëdorovna) was an ancestor of
Frederick II of Prussia.

Among the Soubrys there was a notorious affair, which went back
to the eighteenth century, and which had been the occasion for making
the provocative and sharp change in the language of the family of
Grand Duchess Maria Pavlovna Romanoff, whose husband, Emperor Paul I,
was the most irritable and noxious person who had ever graced the
Russian throne. It existed as a law in the highest circles and served
to impress the Romanoffs, who with their limited talents, were the
most apt for taking revenge on each other.

Grand Duchess Maria Pavlovna Rebecca de Soubry, the Empress Dowager,
says, “I knew that when I was little that the Rohans tormented
the Soubrys, and vice versa. It is a very ancient affair and has been
going on for generations,” and she added, apparently for the sake of
showing her family, that she was informed of a secret which her family
had preserved without ever communicating it to anyone.

The Rohans had been dreaming (so said Grand Duchess Maria Pavlovna
Rebecca) since the eighteenth century that they were said to be
descended from the sons of King Solomon, and that their wife, the
Duchess of Rohan, was actually obtainable through the Soubrys; but
the Soubrys (the Rohans’ ancestors) corresponding with the Rohans, who
pretended to be the descendants of the Rheims branch of the Soubrys,
while the true Soubrys, the ones who had been Soubrys and the heirs
of the duchy, were the descendants of the royal Solomon. They were
said to be “dévotés,” when the Rohans are “sinceros et loyaux.” The
connection, therefore, was to be between the ninth prince and the
Duchess of Rohan—but this connection had not occurred. To make the former
relationship succeed, the son of M. de Soubry de l’Ange in Nantes had been
married a second time to the daughter of the count of Rohan. The son of
the Duchess’ mother, the daughter of the Rohan count’s cousin, daughter
of the Rohan count V. de Rohan, was married to the prince, of whom
Curé de Rohan had been the greatest enemy. It was said that the prince
had died after the birth of his son, and that the child was really
the son of the countess—a wretched child, whom Curé de Rohan was
always treating with disdain.

Grand Duchess Maria Pavlovna’s mother-in-law, the Dowager Empress,
although she had never seen the child herself, spoke of this child as
her own and of the Rohan as her husband. Grand Duchess Maria Pavlovna
Kárámskieva, the wife of Paul I, was furious at all this, and in her
complaints against the dowager she often called the Count of Rohan a
monstrous villain, a reptile, and a creature of the devil. Grand Duchess
Maria Pavlovna was once born into the family—a relationship which had
been cultivated for a thousand years—which was intimately connected
with that of her spouse but which was denied to her by her spouse’s
mother’s father.

The Dowager Empress’s father (the Soubry) was the brother of the
husband of the Countess of Rohan, while it was found out afterwards
that her son was not the son of the prince, who had been Soubry, nor
of the prince’s second wife, who was also the duchess, but the son of
the countess, the daughter of the uncle of the countess, who was also
Soubry. The father of the Duchess of Rohan, the brother of the Soubry
who had been married to the wife of the Rohan, was a real Soubry, while
the son of the Rohan (belonging to the Rohan’s family) was said to
have been a son of the Rohan Queen or the Rohan Princess, the Rohans
claiming that they are of the Rasheims or the Rohans of Rheims. It
was even said that she attended the ceremonies of the confraternity as
the bride of the prince—that is, of the deacon—who was married to the
daughter of the duke of Soubry, the daughter of the deacon.

The Rohans, who had been $500 a year from the Soubrys before the
marriage, agreed to marry and pay for the Rohans’ connection. It was
the dowager who put in her claim of being the daughter of the Rohan and
the mother of the prince of Rohan. It was this dowager who, though she
was not a Soubry, but a wife of the Rohan, was said to be really the
daughter of the Rohan prince and of the Rohan duchess, who owed all the
invisibility of her family to the Rohans in the nineteenth century.

Grand Duchesses Maria Pavlovna’s mother-in-law, the Dowager Empress,
the wife of the Rohan, wrote letters in which she occasionally used
her pseudonym, “the Duchesse de Rohan.” The Rohans imagined that it
was the raw flesh of the bodies of the Soubrys, and that the Soubrys
were dressed for their feasts as vampires. The Rohans therefore were
said to be delivered from the imaginary infection by the reformed
divinity of “divine communion with the Soubrys” by which they were
converted into the Soubrys. The Rohans changed their form and became
the Soubrys; the Soubrys, in their turn, became the Rohans. The Rohans
became an abstract virtue, a state which could only be reached by the
effort of the Prince of France, grandson of the Grand Duke of Rohan and
the Duke of Soubry; and the Rohans were said to be the true proleptic
Soubrys.

The Rohans continued to call themselves Rohans, and the Soubrys,
now renamed Rohans, continued to call themselves the Rohans, while
because the Rohans were not in the habit of adjoining the names in
which they wrote, the Rohans were called the Rohans. The Rohans, being
the Rohans-Leigh, who pretended to be V. de Rohan, who had been a son
of his father, the duke of Soubry, were called “Prologues,” and finally
they ceased to call themselves the Rohans and became the Rohans. The
Soubrys, who had been the Soubrys of the Duchy of the Rohans, and the
Soubrys of Rohan, became the Rohans. The Rohans therefore became the
Soubrys.

The Soubrys imagined that the Rohans were a banded group of the
Soubrys, a brotherhood of the Rohans, and that the Rohans were only
Soubrys who wanted to call themselves Rohans, as the Soubrys were
clever enough to consider that the Rohans were the Soubrys. The Soubrys
imagined that the Rohans, being the Rohans, were so clever that they
could not be able to change their name. The Rohans, who imagined that
they were the Rohans, were called the Soubrys, while the Soubrys were
called the Rohans, and not the Rohans and also the Rohans who did not
delight themselves in calling themselves the Rohans, because the Rohans
were vicious and even the Rohans of the Rohans.

The Rohans continued to be the Rohans, while the Soubrys became the
Leighs, while the Saint-Eulogie became a brotherhood of the Rohans. The
Soubrys who had been the Soubrys of the Rohans were called the Rohans
of the Rohans and the Soubrys of the Soubrys were called the Rohans
because the Soubrys were the brotherhood of the Rohans. Finally, the
true Soubry remained the Soubrys, and, as he who was the Soubrys of
the Soubrys of the Soubrys of “all the Soubrys” was the newcomer to
the Soubrys, he was called the Soubys and, as he was the newcomer to
the Soubrys, he was called the Soubrys, and the Rohans, who were the
Soubrys, were called the Soubrys.

The Rohans were the Soubrys; the Soubrys were the Rohans. The Rohans
continued to be the Rohans, while the Soubrys continued to be the
Soubrys because the Rohans were the Rohans of the Rohans, the Rohans
of the Soubrys, the Rohans of the Soubrys of the Rohans, the Rohans
of the Rohans of the Soubrys, the Rohans of the Rohans of the Rohans,
the Rohans of the Rohans of the Rohans of the Rohans of Soubrys, and
the Rohans were the Soubrys, who were the Soubrys of the Rohans of
the Soubrys, while the Soubrys were the Rohans, and finally—because
the Soubrys were the Rohans—they were the Rohans of the Rohans of the
Rohans, and finally they were also the Rohans, the Soubrys of the
Rohans of the Rohans of the Rohans, the Rohans of the Rohans of the
