Prince Vasíli did not dare to reply. He was not like his daughter,
whose frivolous laughter, artful, careless elegance, and tasteless
foibles, were so irritating to him. He regretted sometimes that at
some future time he must intervene to correct the young girl’s
preoccupation with society, her frivolous manner, and her callous
indifference to everything except herself.

“I know why you want Baron Funke,” went on Anna Pávlovna. “It is
because of your daughter. You will read that she is going to appear
there. Baron Pánin evidently desires to enter the service of the
Empress. Baron Funke, if you like, can do it for you.”

The prince’s lips parted and his face assumed an expression
burdened with suffering. He stammered out:

“Does it belong to me? Do I have any right to speak to my daughter
about this? Did she consent to anything? I don’t see how she intended
to offend the Empress.”

“Why should she?”

“Why shouldn’t she?” he replied. “Could it not be because the Empress
invited Baron Pánin to her private apartments while she was dining and
refused to do the same to me? She told me, however, that the queen
bothered her about that only because of her distaste for the women at
her court.”

“Do you mean to say that your daughter had offended the Empress?”

“My daughter is sixteen!” said the prince irritably. “She cannot have
offended the Empress with people and trifles. She is received not at
all and not at all officially. We do not manage the court and the state
in this way. I repeat, I do not wish to interfere with my daughter. And
did she run any risk? No.”

“You’re not a madman,” said Anna Pávlovna, annoyed, “for sending your
daughter out to people like Baron Funke, who are not even in the
Empress’s confidence. But yes, they play a pleasant game in those
circles.”

“She is a sixteen-year-old girl,” said the prince. “I don’t know
what is going on in those high circles and what I should really
infuriate the Empress, alone by refusing to attend her private dinner
in the Empress’s apartments.”

“Indeed,” said Anna Pávlovna. “But, very dear Prince, consider this:
you have your daughter, who is going to marry Baron Funke, whom you
have just repudiated. What do you think of this?”

The prince, whom she had frightened and shaken, added:

“Yes, I think it a foolish thing to do.”

“Of course. Of course! And that is all,” she said brightly, in an
indifferent tone artificially affected in order, as she herself felt,
“to restore him to calm.”

“Indeed, it is a great mistake.”

“Yes, but I didn’t say that you had made a mistake. It is as if your
daughter wished to become seriously involved with a man of the highest
rank for whom you have no liking at all? What do I say? Is he worth
the trouble incurred?”

“No, indeed,” said the prince. “He is worth nothing! I will tell
you, but he knows better than to give offense to the Empress. He is
received at court and by the Empress.”

“Then, if her Majesty had chosen to free me from my husband, his
grandson, he would have become a very poor, unhappy man because I
refused it. He was a maximally rich man and cannot be said to have done
anything to offend anyone. All I ask of my daughter is that she makes
no mistakes in her future life, that she suffices herself by being a
good girl, becoming a good wife; and that God be all-powerful in the
world. You and your son may go and criticize my daughter’s life, and
that is your affair. I am not going to do it, knowing what she is and
who she is, and what you are. You don’t need to know what it is all
about. You write to her,” she added, with an annoyed smile to him, as
if replying to an idea of his. “And say what you want. Just consider
that you mean to make her suffer greatly if she does not marry Baron
Funke, as you want her to.”

“My daughter will go and marry Baron Funke, without her mother or
father’s consent,” said the prince, placidly, without looking at her.

There were other matters to speak of; the horse race at Kurágs,
Lichtenstein and Talse, and many other women and men whose opinions
concerning them all he did not care to hear. But Anna Pávlovna
incessantly attempted to divert his thoughts from her proposed marriage
by speaking of these trifles, his naval deploy, and the campaign at
the Kurágs. They had been setting off for the palace of the Prince
Bishop to attend a reading from his episcopal chair, when, in a corner
of the chamber, they suddenly interrupted their conversation about the
struck horse in a discussion over the horse-race at Kurágs. The prince
and Anna Pávlovna repeated what the cards of fate had already decided,
as unnoticed witnesses to it.

“Why tell me what you all know?” said the prince. “You have all been
there. Be off!”

“A poor performance!” replied Anna Pávlovna in a tone of false
centenarian ignorance, ill-adapted to her precocious knowledge.

What was it that the horse had begun to do again and again, after
he had just buried his head in the neck of the poor Curie, and which
caused Prince Vasíli such a strong dislike of the course? The horse
seemed to have lost its natural and tranquil spirit, and if Rezonim
succeeded in turn to calm it, Kurágin still remained for a time
utterly unconvincing and made the riders of the old and the young
struck together mingle in dismay and confusion.

When they came to the turn, the prince said nothing. It was just then
that the horse seemed to him like a runaway horse in a slaughterhouse;
it neighed and whipped its tail, drove its heels into the ground, and
presumably was out of its senses. All persons connected with the horse
raced after it, each horseman striving frantically to reach it. Prince
Kurágin, who rode with the Curie, never had the smallest memory or
clear notion of what he was doing. Anna Pávlovna continued speaking
with her usual assurance. A colonel from Kuliginsky regiment, on the
contrary, had a dalliance with the broken hearted Prísná, the deadly
sufferer, a red-haired youth, taken recently not from the Dnieper but
from the Western camps. Anna Pávlovna was fond of saying that she saw
Kuliginsky in the immediate future marrying a beautiful Curie. The
Colonne in particular, the small horse of the old man, the father of
the young lady who was the assistant to Elísaveta Kurátskaya, proved
the weakness of the young horse; the former could not have felt any
despair if he had heard the next words uttered by the young object of
all the admiration, which was evident in the fact that he would have
laughed.

“And to such a horse, my dear, did Konstantín ride?” said the
prince.

“Indeed,” replied Anna Pávlovna, then regaining herself and adopting
a more tranquil tone, “to such a horse the scullery-scavengers of the
Bursà found a new science. Gronski for instance, riding Lion and
Centaur, was such a valiant rider that the exhibition of the horse
was destroyed by the excess of the riders’ enthusiasm. Gronski had all
the audacity, the Decius Mus of the horse-races. That is all. I wish
you and those who have been there fewer misadventures.”

Prince Vasíli said nothing, contenting himself with smiling at the
spectacle, and nearly the first man to laugh over his own suffering,
wished to keep the well-being of the him and his son and see the good
result of the horse race on the side of the church. He disliked Kurágs
and wished it to disappear. A Rus’ never has a disposition for anything
which reminds him of military discipline; he is afraid of It and dislikes
it. He is a humorist by nature and is capable of an optical illusion
which enables him to eliminate all things he has not made, or that he
does not want, to exist. For this reason he frequently enjoyed
becoming the sport of others. Anna Pávlovna, on the other hand, from
the first moment of the race till its terrible catastrophe, had the
impression that the beach and the horse-races had never existed, and even
after the accident, despaired of Kurágs, and, remembering that the
suffering and indignation of others tasted like brimstone to her pride,
could only smile and sadly express her satisfaction.

But the principle of self-abnegation, which was the quality that
always, though not very coherently, distinguished Prince Vasíli on his
long platform of social existence, his kind and beneficent reduplication
of his wife, and his distinct lack of egoism, could not fail, at some
time, to take a hasty and incorrect turn. The prince became too
sensitive from over-exposure. The assaults of jealousy and spite grew
frequent. He withdrew himself and began to examine everything afresh and
make himself difficult, as a result of which, each day bringing him a
fresh source of disappointment, he slowly ceased to care about the
implications of any social action and became as red in the face as the
King of Prussia.

Meanwhile the attentions of Baron Funke toward his daughter were soon
revealed. On a certain day, on seeing the Empress, Mr. and Mrs. Funke
behaved with such unrestrained free-speech that the conduct of this
highly placed couple aroused suspicion, as a rule it does.

René, a self-possessed man, of his nature and according to the
traditions of his family, considered himself free and independent
from the bench of the Empress; he even went so far as to laugh at
her appointments. He was to say, I guess, in a twenty-four-hours
rigorous confinement, alma frater ex albo majis—is there a better
word than this in the French tongue? Alma frater ex albo majis. The
Pánins were going to him in great numbers, quite naturally. He was
encamped at the Court at home, and its little comity was beginning to
grow.

And his daughter was becoming dizzy. She told nothing of what she
understood, nor her own aspirations, believing it was the duty of her
silly parents to arrange and select everything for her. Her mind
gravitated spontaneously toward high objects; she did not know why this
was the case and even laughed at herself. Baron Funke, however,
weighed the conscience of her parents even more lightly, and not
suspecting everything, as she suspected, she began to wonder and
resent, and not without cause, the more so as it concerned her father,
the constant and ardent objective of her destiny. Though she did not
know or care, Bogdan Pánin coveted in her some of those traits which
seemed to him so dear to him or to the Duc de Service, the Emperor
Alexander.

The Baroness and the Countess stood like giants in the abyss with
their hands on their backs, understanding nothing, contenting
themselves with gratifying their family pride, and not noticing that
they were occupied with the ruthless rearing of a costly engine. The
Countess, a curmudgeon, bemoaned the fact that her husband gave, with
his and her daughter’s consent, no acknowledgment whatever to the
Empress’s choice of her son-in-law. Velýkíy Fédor, as she called
himself, wailed about our Empress being a better judge than her husband
or Baron Funke, as the Empress called him.

She alone diverted her mind by the fact that Baron Funke had been
received at her court, and suggested that the Commission could not
be ‘received.’

It was, however, Baron Funke, who was against his will, the only man
not to be surled, the most animated man in creation, who proved
herself a good choice.

In the same way Father Pieraccini and Father Borghese thus commenced
their unhappy fate.

It is not superstition, but true science, that has invented this
invisible doping of the brain and spoken of the most weightless
mistakes. It was a little after the twenty-third, or the nineteenth,
year of the Empire. In the world she was already good, which was
astonishing as was the fact that no one suspected it. By the influence
and grace of the Empress’s Court, the Dowager Empress Márya Fëdorovna
(requisitioned by the Empress’s father-in-law as a fruit of the Empress’s
beneficent patronage), the Dowager Empress had been named Imperial
Nun, and drank tea with the Empress, also becoming her friend. The
Emperor, however, did not love her, nor did she love him, and her
respect for him never reached the Duc de Service, the Emperor
Alexander.

Prince Vasíli Kurágin became furious, thinking of the other people who
had come to him and had pronounced in favor of his daughter while he
himself reproved them.

“I am not grateful to those who support my daughter?” he said. “I
will not forgive them. I will not write to them. I will not allow my
daughter to marry a man whom she does not love.”

Mrs. Schérer was astonished and thought he was somewhat boastful for
a moment. “Why can’t you see,” said she, “that the educa... I mean
that the female education best suited your daughter for a man like
that?”

“Exactly what do you mean, my dear? Do you suppose my daughter ever
would have gone and married Baron Funke? I will not marry her off to
anyone she does not love.”

“We needn’t doubt it. One doesn’t know what one does for these
prickly people. Who will say one thing if nothing happens, owing to the
unluckiness of the moment. This scurvy Pánin, for example, is still
in our sincere confidence. My dear prince, this is absurd! You should
have seen at the Курágs the two Florians. They are near death, or at
least will come to death, in spite of the sufferings, the patience
and the endurance of the family. Oh, very good; but see this.... My
father caught a cold and died of it, and still he aged with such
enjoyment which, may it be, will not go far and will not be long with
us.”

After that the prince sent to Fôria and the post of the shawl
“passed” not at all to his son. The baroness received everyone, but the
commissions for the Princess’s apartment and, especially for the
Empress’s, were always to her.

The Prince soon became ill, and that was the last of his utmost
displeasure. He, however, did not say this, and even less talk about
what would be to the Empress. Nevertheless, the refusal of the baron
to inform him was an act of too great a breach of confidence. The
Prince, neither the least distrustful, nor even the least cold, like
Anna Pávlovna, accused him secretly of the mal-intention of not
particularly seeking his permission to the baron and not put on guard
for him or for himself.

“Yes, I am a very good man. I give my daughter up for the
Empress’s pleasure. And I will say it again—I have not a dislike for
people, not even for the Russian seigneur Baron Funke.”

With his whole soul and his whole nature, the Prince wished to see his
daughter marry this man, or one like him, before whom, according to
him, there were no significant obstacles. And so Prince Vasíli
Kurágin, in spite of himself, had for his daughter a most natural,
most sonorous, most intuitive, most spontaneously held opinion, which
evoked the inevitable reaction of judgment. He passed on to others,
unconsciously, the confidence which he had no wish to share; he
confidently said to his daughter, as if he had not a motive to say
even the admittance that he gave her hardly deserves the Empress’s
grace.

When Prince Vasíli saw his daughter in the Empress’s company, he felt
his resentment and his sorrow subsided. Even the paternal pain which
could never pass right through his heart appeared like a shadow, and
his love, which dwelt in him forever, like an instinct, remained the
only thought of his child. Soon he noticed that his daughter was only in
the room of the Empress and Baron Funke, and on reading the
commissions of this annoyance was kept.

“Dear wife,” said he to Mrs. Schérer once. “Tell your people by all
means to note the grave mistakes of our dear prince, Baron Pánin, that
his son is close to the Empress, and that if he is to be sent to
Canada, however vast the content, he will be disappointed. His friends
have incomprehensibly and absurdly believed that my youth is petering
out, and I have thought of nothing but of my initials, but I now cannot
help renewing my faith in them. Baron Pánin, who has great ambitions,
sees our daughter almost at the Empire and is going to marry her to a
man for whom she has no preferences. And I have once again thought
only of our initials.”

He could not reveal his grief. It placed him not only in sorrow, but
also punished him for the laziness and ease of his life, for the
inssecurity of his integrity, in that he dared to think and judge
freely, without being tied by the customs and traditions of the society
to which he belonged.

message came from her:

“As Princess Curie has so attently waited on me with her face, as I
asked you to invite her, and as the visit has been made, I send a
pack of cards for her in the interest of my high regard.”

Prince Vasíli, dying of jealousy, went to the Empress, and, fearing
lesser communications, wished to see the Empress. Baron Pánin, who was
in the Empress’s company, was not allowed to enter. In his absence the
Empress took in the cards, which he would have taken if he had known

custom or his paternal duty or simply by his lack of desire for his
daughter to be misleadingly named, went to the Empress with his
daughter, this time, not on the pretext of the woman, that she had
come a good distance and could not return to the Epitaphium until
another day.

She spoke with that melancholy irony of another age which did not
belong to her, but which she copied from her great-grandmothers. She
felt that her lack of true love for her children was an injustice, that
it was unworthy of her, though she did not wish to admit it. She was
delighted to hear him say:

“Marlowe, the Countess de Mortemart’s brother, is coming with
her to see her cousin.”

“Yes, I know that. And Viskytsa is coming with him.”

“Viskyta? Why Viskyta and not a Refugee?” asked the prince,
disconcerted.

“I told you no Refugees are coming. Viskyta, I told you, is coming
with the Countess,” said Anna Pávlovna, almost resentful.

“Viskyta is an introduced lady, and to come to the Embassy is
sheer lunacy,” said the prince in a burlesque tone, which Madame
Schérer found perfectly natural to him.

“Don’t laugh, Prince! And Morio will be coming, too.”

“It’s fine to have so many people,” said the prince, though he did
not feel so indecent as to laugh. “I really must not forget to
tell Grand Duchess Maria,” as if she would help her get rid of
them.

“Oh, she is so good! She will not say a word in her favor against
that woman of the young refugees,” grumbled Anna Pávlovna.

“Won’t she?” exclaimed the prince, half laughing. “How is it
seems to me that you do not wish for me to have the refugees in the
world, though you are still exchanging眼睛里 с ними
любопытных словечек!”

“Don’t be absurd! Anatole and Alexandrine are the best
refugees. In them you must still have faith.”

“Faith? Faith in my poor Anatole and Alexandrine! And how do you
explain the change in your politics? First the joint declaration of
all the émigrés. Your letter to those who are not in government. Let
me say, Madame Schérer, you are not a loyal subject!”

“Loyal is not synonymous with faithful. Loyal is the duty of the
subject, faithful the duty of the friend.”

“Belongs to a new term. Since the death of Napoleon there have been
no loyal subjects. One can not be loyal to an evil empire.”

“The Russian Empire is not evil,” said Anna Pávlovna, taking her
comfort from the ignorance of the prince. “What matters? You were
always as you are, he said. If Prussia had always been like
Prussia....”

And while she cried in this fashion she reached for the tea.

The prince smiled, as if to say: “Who is not seriously injured
nowadays by such serious remarks as these?”

And he took Anna Pávlovna’s hand, saying:

“Now tell me, what can one do to console me? I curse my fate. But
I don’t want it to look as if I cursed it.”

Anna Pávlovna had become accustomed to people’s taking advantage
of her enthusiasm, her unbounded admiration of our Emperor Alexander,
and her sincere piety, to ask questions. But tonight she wished to
give a lesson in royal virtues. Her dead sister, the Dowager Empress,
was the one familiar with Alexander, the one who could explain him,
the only one competent to speak of him.

“Does your son ever come to see the Emperor? I am sure he does. And
he is going to do it soon.”

The prince bowed with perfect courtesy and readiness.

“My son,” said Anna Pávlovna, “is an extraordinary young man. He
of course does very little to win the Emperor’s confidence. All that
God has given him, he has not helped to secure. But, despite this, he
is an extraordinary young man. He speaks with complete naturalness and
confidence. He has a deep, though not very high, voice, and, what
is more, a special expression of face, nothing like the numerous
veritable idols of the dance. He has a peculiar glance, which one
describes as a glance altogether, more precisely—a glance of a man
who has been living in the wilderness.”

“The Emperor is very disposed to listen to him,” said the prince.
“I always see him sitting down to dinner with the Emperor, having quite
a good time.”

“But did you see him?” said Anna Pávlovna. “I will ask our Empress
to-day for an introduction for him.... This is what I think first,
that he is an extraordinary young man. I would like him to have his
eyes opened. That’s all I can say. I can’t say anything else. Anyhow
the Emperor is listening to him, and I believe what he says,” she
added, with a cerise flush playing round her lips. “The Emperor,
indeed, is listening to him!” she added again, with the same flush
and a particular affectation. “When he—” She suddenly paused, but
the embarrassed smile which alternately played round her lips proved
that she did not feel herself very worthy to hear the King of Prussia
in the same place as the Emperor. The prince had not introduced her
much to the Emperor. She really had not done her best to procure an
introduction. But it was true that Prince Vasíli’s son had come to
dinner with the Emperor regularly, and had been praised by him. He
was usually presented to the Empress previous to her seeing the
Emperor.

Anna Pávlovna added:

“He has the Emperor’s confidence. And his Majesty told me that he
seems to know everything. That is something he has in common with
the Emperor.”

“Who?” said the prince.

“With the Emperor. He knows everything!” she repeated with emphasis.

Prince Vasíli washed his hands in honor of the evening’s fete, and
later, in the emperor’s palace, he went to the reception of the
Countess Bálenoff, which was one of the most important fêtes in
St. Petersburg.

Great events, according to the principle of the phases of the moon,
are ushered in by a period of calm and quiet. The atmosphere of the
great diplomatic Congress at Vienna, and of the formidable opposition
formed by European sovereigns against the encroachments of Napoleon’s
boot, is throwing its shadow over the palaces of the Empress and her
family. On the night of the fete there was a veritable calm. The
whole city was whispering that Buonaparte had not aimed at war with
Europe but had despaired of it, like the wise man who, while holding
the lance against the hydra of revolution, had confided it to a worthy
peasant who had entered into a pact with him for its destruction. A
murmur was not without reason. The aforesaid conversation with Prince
Vasíli had given rise to a strong impression throughout St. Petersburg.

Of the guests who came to the Countess Bálenoff’s ball Anna Pávlovna
Schérer mentioned the most interesting. She felt that the Vicomte de
Mortemart was coming from Leghorn. He had been received by the
Emperor. The Vicomte had been among the first to break the news
of his arrival to her. And he was coming fourth-class, with
Sustchev, who, on his return from Rome, would make his court. The
Vicomte had been received by the Emperor Alexander and the Dowager
Empress by Novosíltsev at St. Peter’s. The Abbé Morio, an Italian
professor, had been received by the Emperor at the Hotel Molitore
and carried to his lodgings by the Dowager Empress. The Abbé Morio
was a man of merit, of a gloomy temperament, who had written many
books on metaphysics. It was said that he had especially written
one of the finest of all those works. But there was not the least
resemblance between this man and his portrait. A very fair, thin,
dandyish head, long curls, a fondness for long riding clothes, an
out-and-out indolence, were the marks by which he was characterized.
The Abbé Morio’s case was somewhat different from that of his
comet. There were several opposing opinions: some declared that the
Emperor Alexander’s reception was the result, others that it was the
beginning. Initially, however, the idea prevailed that Morio had been
received by surprise.

It was the month of July, 1805. The meteor which had burst at the
beginning of summer was disappearing toward the end of it. The Prince of
the Condé had gone into retirement; the liberal movement had ceased
vividly, and Jacobins were no longer a cause celebre. The cherry tree
of Revolution was slowly dying. The Supreme Council of Government
had come from exile; Ludovia’s star had begun to rise, but its rays
did not yet fall on France. On the contrary, it was said that the
Dowager Empress had been dissatisfied with the homage of which she had
received the Abbé Morio. A recent artist had just completed the
portrait of the Empress from life. Her Majesty had been frightened that
the picture might injure the Empress’s reputation. She had ordered
that a hole be made in the picture that the artist knew well. Even
the artist was not among the many who admired the picture.

At the latest the Abbé Morio had been introduced to the newcomer,
an Italian painter, Mariani, who had arrived in Petersburg with
his head shaved and hidden under a bandana. Mariani had confirmed
the emperor’s words to the Dowager Empress and to the Empress
herself. The Dowager Empress, who had deceived herself into thinking
that Morio had come to the court of Russia because of his learning,
was not a believer in the poetic prowess of the painter.

The Dowager Empress, in the meantime, had only been waiting to debate
with Morio the merits of the three principal painters. In her view
Mariani and Morio had nothing in common with Raphael, but the Italians
would like to exterminate the old works of the Renaissance, and the
French to prefer their native painters to the Italian masters.

Mariani had said:

“It is impossible to teach painting in this country.”

The Dowager Empress had replied:

“Yes, but we do not own our paintings.”

The Empress Maria Feodorovna had expressed herself very politely and
said:

“I also have my favorite painters.”

Of course Mariani had seen the portrait of the Empress and had
attacked the Dowager Empress. In his opinion she was only an
illiterate. On the contrary, Morio, an austere intellectual, had
declared that the Empress’s portraits were the most charming in the
world.

The Dowager Empress had invited the Abbé Morio to have dinner with
him. Morio had declined with a conscientious indecision. Morio’s
conscientiousness was a quality respected in Russia, but it was
insufferable to the dwellers in Petersburg who were accustomed to
superficiality. The Abbé was a man who had been forgotten in his own
country and who, after a series of failures, had come to Russia in
the hope of making some profit. He certainly did not stand out
among the fashionable curio curiosities of the house of Romanoff. His
landlord at the Hotel Molitore, however, Mr. Housruff, was said to
be a rich man and where a man is rich, there is at least one friend.
The Abbé Morio, however, was not among Housruff’s friends.

In the midst of all these events Mariani was mysteriously advancing
toward the Empress, and Morio, an old acquaintance and admirer of the
Dowager Empress, was trying to come to her rescue. Mariani and Morio
were very different, not only in character and in their position in
society, but also in striking contrasts. Mariani’s portrait, painted
by Morio, was quite a success. It made a great impression, not merely
at the Imperial headquarters, but even among the people, who had been
delighted to see the living Empress Michaelii Fonovezova painted by
Mariani. A competition was opened in the public galleries, and the
weeping and lamentations, especially by the ladies and their maidens,
were impressive. Mariani’s portrait was hung on the wall of the Palace
of the Empress, but it was among the paintings at the Hotel Molitore,
which had already been sold.

Mariani’s success must be attributed to his pictorial representation
of a slight vocation or passion that was dear to the Empress. She
was not very fond of the Abbé Morio, and Mariani had painted her
carrying the infanta, as she claimed to be, on the sea in a boat,
feeling the excitement of galloping horses, and lounging on the banks
of the river with her ribbon pin drawn round her neck.¹ Mariani
had also painted her in the costume of the Empress Dowager, and
dressed her in a red silk dressing gown, with her hair pulled back
and her head shaved. There was something macabre even in the
empertinent haughtiness with which she loomed up from either of
the tombstones, which were supplied by Simon Kamenski, the pallor
of whose skin corresponded to her own.

But in the intermediate situations she became charming. These likenesses
were said to be, like the Empress herself, the truest and the most
perfect. Mariani, one of the most distinguished men of the age, had
a distinguished wife, the daughter of the Grand Dukeof Tallinn, and
his mother’s cousin, and he was very rich. Mariani shared his art
with his wife Angelina, who was one of the most talented women in
Russia. The Empress was greatly moved by the enthusiasm of pagan
animals in painting Mariani, but the Abbé Morio had painted an
extraordinary portrait of the Empress that exhibited her unique
personality. Mariani said:

“I would much rather have her shrine in Holland on the sea in a
boat than this portrait of her in the red dressing gown.”

The Empress was pleased with Morio’s portrait. Mariani would have
liked to see her in Holland. The two had a quarrel. Morio had been
correct and faithful in his likenesses, and Mariani had portraited
the Empress outside herself—according to Peter the Great’s portrait,
with a horse in the background.

Mariani’s technique was entirely different from that of Morio. The latter
was indiscriminately truthful and the former fictitious. The Empress
and Morio were both brought to the palace to attend the Empress. The
portrait of the Empress Widow had first been done by Morio, and only
later by Mariani. Mariani had said it must be painted in both poses:
sitting and standing. Morio had objected that the round, fleshy
forehead of the Empress, wearing a white Persian turban, tinged by
the sun, was too unnatural. Morio was justified by the findings of
medical scientists. Morio ridiculed his rival’s portraits of the Empress
as the Emperor Alexander’s portrait of Baroness de Swetchine, and the
former complained that Morio’s portrait of the Empress resembled
the Empress Dawager’s portrait of her half-brother. Morio had said
that he had seen the Empress herself, but Mariani had admitted that
he had not seen the Empress in her own house, or or in the Hotel
Molitore, but in the hotel of another Mariani. Mariani’s admiring
glance was curious and not very flattering.

One day Mariani was walking in a garden. He saw while passing over
some lilies in the flower bed that they looked like little girls
with white heads. Scholars, even accounts, contradicted him that
lilies were the emblem of the Empress and that Mariani could not have
taken them to represent a neat little girl. The Empress had said that
lilies were the emblem of her beauty. She could not have been a little
girl, and she was much older than lilies. In another garden she saw
angel-trees growing and Mariani had caught an exciting thought that
the Empress was like an angel. Mariani had said that he had never
saw the Empress when she stood in front of an angel-tree and had judged
her to be neither an angel nor a little girl. The Empress, however, had
asked him to show him Morio’s portrait of the Empress when she had
stood in front of an angel-tree, and Mariani had said that he believed
Morio had seen her in that position.

In October, 1805, Morio arrived in St. Petersburg and secretly
visited the Empress. The Empress had told Mariani what he had said
later. Morio had said that the Empress was a repetition of the Empress
Dowager. Mariani had seen Morio’s portrait. Mariani had said Morio
had painted the Empress as she had stood in front of the angel-tree.
The Empress had said, in an angry tone, that she preferred Mariani’s
version and that Morio had painted her as he had seen her. The
portrait of the Empress Widow showed her with a horse in the background.
In fact, Morio’s portrait bore almost no resemblance to that of the
Empress herself.

Some of the lady visitors to the Empress recognized her in her
portrait. They had talked about Mariani. The portrait of the Empress
Widow was not exposed at the Hotel Molitore because, as Morio said,

A cross expression crossed the prince’s face as if he had accepted
this share of blame.

“Why look at me like that?” he asked in a whisper, assuming his
placid expression. Anna Pávlovna, whose voice had not yet subsided,
continuing:

“It seems to me that you don’t have time to look at your children. No,
you don’t, remember that just as well as I do.”

“I sincerely love my sons and my daughter. My days are very short,
risen like the sun from the East and set like the sun in the West,” He
drew his hands across his face. “They did not live long. Hamed the
first left me one year ago.... I phlegmatism, health, and an excessive
reverence for the present, all desire my attention to be so occupied
and thrown into relief as to keep the impression of my children from
reaching me to a very slight degree!”

He added these words not even betraying any thought that he was talking
of his children. But when Anna Pávlovna heard her husband say this
without seriousness, carelessness, or exaggeration, and listened to
the magnanimous tone with which he comforted all his wrongs—she felt
him to be a princely man, but then, as is natural to a woman, she
restored to her husband his son, and persuaded herself that the Prince
had accused her that she did not love him, his father. She looked at
him and said:

“You accuse me, Father?”

And now she began to speak of her own children. They were six. They
had been born to a rich woman, and one of her handmaidens had been
secretly very fond of one of Pirof’s sons who, in spite of others,
came frequently to her to play for her. The handmaiden was one of those
who are naturally and permanently gifted with feminine ardor, tender
affection, and capacity for secret affection. The echo of Pirof’s
smiles troubled no one but the handmaiden and a veiled friend who was
the handmaiden’s mistress. In the following spring the handmaiden
and her mistress had each given birth to a child. The cannibal side of
the handmaiden’s mother treated the second child, who hissed more than
garlic making, by torture instead of family love. Her father the gambler
sold the child to an intrigante who made sure, one year later, that he
might be worn for the good of the family, washed him, and bathed him in
aromatic glycerine. She never saw Pirof, and him as a man she had
known but two years, and her grandson she thought he resembled
untenable, Usexust etc. her. “What was the daughter to do?” continued
the handmaiden. “And now my son is a dwarf, and my daughter, whom I
treasured (and do treasure) for another generation, is lost to me. As
for the hope of having 69.27 children—one cannot always have obtained
the much-desired grandchildren by virtue of the active working of the
principle of birthing.”

"We have six,” said the Prince. Anna Pávlovna, sitting in the
chair-appointed for him, outlined him and his son as a child at
the age of four on a faint slip of paper with elegant sloping strokes:

Princes and princesses were enemies. During all the few days of
friendship which left its trace on Prince Vasíli’s memories, his
feelings for公爵公爵公爵’s daughters had been dreams; they were
almost as devoid of reality as the emotions arising from his intimacy
with Anna Pávlovna Schérer. By his profession as a courtier he knew
superficially as well as how to carry out the conventionalities of
love. The set conventions of literary Bildung, combining tender with
demanding passion, had given him a taste for these dreams and a
satisfaction in his imaginary poems and characters. He would have to
conceive them again, in detail, or imitate them with infinite
carefulness as he was doing at the present moment, to be fit publisher
and proponent of his fathers’ ideas. The smile which played on
the one side of Prince Vasíli’s lips, only now less tender and less
confidential in proportion as his free and loved dream did not seem so
passionate, encouraged this impression.
